subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is an electrolyte?
options: A molten or aqueous ionic compound that conducts electricity and is broken down by it
A metal wire that carries current into the cell
A covalent liquid that conducts electricity without decomposing
Any solid that allows electrons to pass through it
questions.explain: An electrolyte is an ionic compound, molten or in aqueous solution, that conducts electricity and is decomposed during electrolysis.

questions.q: In electrolysis, the negative electrode is called the:
questions.explain: The cathode is the negative electrode, to which positive ions (cations) are attracted.

questions.q: Which pair of materials is commonly used to make inert electrodes?
questions.explain: Platinum and carbon (graphite) are unreactive, so they are used as inert electrodes that do not take part in the reactions.

questions.q: During electrolysis, positively charged ions (cations) move towards the:
questions.explain: Cations are attracted to the negative electrode, the cathode, where they gain electrons.

questions.q: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved in water before it can be electrolysed?
options: So that the ions are free to move and carry charge to the electrodes
So that the compound becomes a covalent liquid
So that electrons can flow through the solid lattice
So that the compound reacts with the electrodes
questions.explain: In a solid the ions are fixed in a lattice; melting or dissolving frees the ions so they can move and conduct electricity.

questions.q: At the cathode, ions gain electrons. This type of reaction is called:
questions.explain: Gain of electrons is reduction, which always occurs at the cathode.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes what happens at the anode during electrolysis?
options: Negative ions lose electrons, so oxidation occurs
Positive ions gain electrons, so reduction occurs
Electrons are gained, so oxidation occurs
questions.explain: At the positive anode, anions lose electrons; loss of electrons is oxidation.

questions.q: When molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed, the product formed at the cathode is:
questions.explain: Lead ions (Pb²⁺) are attracted to the cathode where they gain electrons to form lead metal.

questions.q: When molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed, the product formed at the anode is:
questions.explain: Bromide ions (Br⁻) move to the anode, lose electrons and form bromine.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, the gas produced at the cathode is:
questions.explain: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen from the water is discharged at the cathode instead of sodium.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, the gas produced at the anode is:
questions.explain: With a concentrated chloride solution, chloride ions are discharged in preference to hydroxide, giving chlorine at the anode.

questions.q: After electrolysing concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, which substance remains dissolved in the solution?
questions.explain: As hydrogen and chloride ions are removed, sodium ions and hydroxide ions are left, forming sodium hydroxide solution.

questions.q: When dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes, the volumes of hydrogen and oxygen collected are in the ratio:
questions.explain: Twice the volume of hydrogen is produced at the cathode compared with oxygen at the anode, reflecting the formula of water, H₂O.

questions.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using inert carbon electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
questions.explain: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are discharged and copper metal is deposited on the cathode.

questions.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using inert carbon electrodes. What forms at the anode?
questions.explain: Sulfate ions are not discharged, so hydroxide ions from the water are oxidised to give oxygen at the anode.

questions.q: Which half-equation correctly represents the discharge of hydrogen at the cathode?
questions.explain: Two hydrogen ions each gain one electron (reduction) to form one hydrogen molecule.

questions.q: Which half-equation correctly represents the formation of chlorine at the anode?
questions.explain: Two chloride ions each lose one electron (oxidation) to form one chlorine molecule.

questions.q: What is the overall reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.explain: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water, releasing energy as electricity.

questions.q: Which is a key advantage of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell compared with burning petrol in an engine?
options: Its only chemical product is water, so it does not release pollutants
It produces large amounts of carbon dioxide
It works without any supply of oxygen
It stores energy as a solid fuel
questions.explain: The fuel cell produces only water, avoiding the polluting gases released when fossil fuels are burned.

questions.q: A metal spoon is to be electroplated with silver. During the process the spoon should be connected as the:
questions.explain: The object being plated is made the cathode so that metal ions are reduced and deposited onto its surface.
